text:
Continuing the varietal survey, this section of the chapter elaborates on the practical differences between the two main flesh-type categories introduced earlier — firm/crisp-fleshed types and soft/very sweet-fleshed types — and how growers and traders use these to decide how a given tree's fruit should be marketed. Firm-fleshed types hold their shape well when cut, travel and store better, and are generally preferred for retail sale as prepared/sliced flesh because the segments separate cleanly from the rind and core. Soft-fleshed types are typically sweeter and more aromatic but bruise and spoil faster, are harder to slice cleanly, and are more often consumed at home or sold whole near the point of harvest rather than shipped to distant markets.

The text also describes typical differences in tree architecture and fruiting habit between named types: some varieties are noted for bearing fruit low on the trunk and main branches (a trait valued for ease of harvest and for allowing more fruit to be supported without branch breakage), while others bear more fruit higher in the canopy. Fruit size, rind spine coarseness, and number of fruit per bunch/cluster are also used descriptively to help identify named varieties in the field.

The chapter reiterates a practical recommendation that appears repeatedly through the book: because jackfruit trees grown from seed are highly variable and often disappointing in fruit quality compared to the parent tree, farmers wanting a specific known variety should obtain grafted, budded, or air-layered (marcotted) planting material taken from a mother tree of confirmed good quality, rather than relying on seedlings, and should ideally observe a mother tree's fruit over at least one full bearing cycle before taking propagation material from it.
